title: An 11-Day-Old Baby Couldn’t Stop Bleeding. For Hours, the ER Didn’t Provide a Critical Vitamin Shot.
author: Duaa Eldeib
content:
The emergency room was a mile from their Texas home. Stephanie and Eric
Biesenbach took comfort in that when their newborn daughter, Gwen, wouldn’t
stop bleeding from her belly button. They buckled Gwen into her car seat and
made the drive over.

Medical records from that warm August evening in 2023 described her condition
as a “generic problem” of a bleeding umbilical cord stump. The doctor on duty,
Nicole Malouf, had treated plenty of those as an emergency room specialist.
She covered Gwen’s oozing belly button with a special gauze to stanch the
flow, and when it appeared to stop, she sent Stephanie, Eric and Gwen on their
way.

They made it as far as the parking lot before they noticed Gwen had bled
through her footed pajamas. Eric slid his arm under the car seat handle and
lifted his 11-day-old daughter out of the car. They walked back toward the
glaring lights of the Lonestar 24HR ER, a freestanding emergency department in
New Braunfels next to a car wash, a McDonald’s and a deli.

Stephanie told Malouf that Gwen had been bleeding a bit after the scab that
replaced her umbilical cord stump fell off. The amount of blood they saw that
night worried them. She ticked through Gwen’s history. No fever. No vomiting.
Exclusively breastfed. She mentioned that she and Eric had declined a vitamin
K shot when Gwen was born and instead had been giving Gwen oral vitamin K
drops, which they trusted would protect her.

Malouf tried another type of pretreated gauze. When that didn’t work, medical
records show, she turned to silver nitrate, a chemical applied to the tip of a
long matchlike stick that cauterizes blood vessels. Malouf rotated one stick
after another inside Gwen’s belly button.

Since the 1960s, the vast majority of newborns in the United States have
received a vitamin K shot. The injection virtually eliminated vitamin K
deficiency bleeding, a rare condition that can cause catastrophic bleeding and
even death.

But a shift in recent years has threatened to upend the unwavering protection
that many doctors and hospitals had taken for granted. Families — mistrustful
of medical interventions, misled by social media and devoted to a birth
experience they deem natural — have begun to shun the vitamin K shot.

A
[pair](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2856300?guestAccessKey=1e1881c3-7eea-4aa4-875c-bb50b32b352b)
of
[studies](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2856352?guestAccessKey=96bb1e40-9080-4a62-ba58-d3fdf4e3e652)
published last week, both of which involved millions of births, found that
babies who didn’t get the vitamin K shot had an increased risk of bleeding.
[One of the
studies](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2856352?guestAccessKey=96bb1e40-9080-4a62-ba58-d3fdf4e3e652)
found that between 2017 and 2025, the rate of vitamin K deficiency bleeding
increased a staggering 347%.

Without the single, inexpensive shot — which is not a vaccine — [babies are
dying](https://www.propublica.org/article/more-parents-decline-vitamin-k-shot-
newborns). Autopsies reveal how babies’ systems shut down without warning and
well-meaning parents who declined the vitamin K shot were left mourning the
loss of their children.

Malouf kept trying to stop the bleeding. Over the course of nearly three
hours, she used seven methods. At one point, she applied so much pressure to a
bandage that, Stephanie said, Gwen threw up. The remedies essentially treated
the symptoms and not the cause, like putting a cover on a leaking faucet.

Malouf said she called her husband, who’s also a doctor, as well as a nurse at
a local hospital, to see if she was missing something. They, too, were at a
loss. The nurse’s only suggestions were the ones that Malouf had already
tried.

Malouf decided to transfer Gwen to a small, local hospital, which at least had
pediatric specialists and a neonatal intensive care unit. But while she waited
for a call back to confirm the hospital would accept Gwen, Stephanie walked
out of the room to tell her that Gwen had bled through the latest dressing.
Malouf, according to the records, quickly checked to see how long it was
taking her blood vessels to refill. It was slower than when she arrived.

Gwen’s condition was growing more dire, and Malouf had reached the limits of
what she could do. What followed also wouldn’t be enough.

![The exterior of a modern 24/7 standalone emergency medical facility under a
blue sky. ](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260810-Bazan-
VitaminK-018_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)Stephanie
and Eric Biesenbach took Gwen to an emergency room a mile from their house.
Brenda Bazán for ProPublica

* * *

Stephanie had given birth to Gwen without complications in an inflatable tub
in their living room. She was perfect, with doelike eyes and a full head of
brown hair that, when the light hit it, hinted at the red of her father’s
beard.

Her older brothers and sisters fussed over her like a birthday present. Her
aunts from California and Louisiana came in to meet her. When the house
quieted, Gwen fell asleep to the calming rhythm of Stephanie’s chest rising
and falling.

Stephanie marveled at the way Gwen seemed to study the faces of everyone who
carried her. She wasn’t two weeks yet, but the corners of her mouth constantly
turned up to form what her parents insisted were smiles. Even when her
siblings passed her around, she rarely cried in protest.

Stephanie and Eric met in 2010, when they both worked at Chili’s. Texas
natives, they had just returned home after spending time in Florida, where
Stephanie spent a semester interning at Walt Disney World Resort.

“I was doing lawn care work and maintenance on restaurants,” Eric said before
Stephanie interjected. “He moved there for a girl,” she said as the two
erupted in laughter.

He proposed to Stephanie on Christmas Eve. They married at a vineyard on
Halloween. The venue capped off the night with fireworks.

Life moved quickly after that. They had a daughter and two sons, then adopted
the daughter of a relative who was too young to care for the child herself.
Just when they thought their family was complete, Stephanie got pregnant with
Gwen.

Overjoyed, they decided to name her after Stephanie’s grandmother, Gwendolyn,
who passed down her flowered baby blanket with “Gwen” embroidered in the
corner.

There were no signs something could be wrong with Gwen until the day her
parents took her to the ER. Stephanie had texted her midwife first.

“So sorry to bother you,” she typed into her phone, writing that Gwen’s belly
button had been bleeding most of the day and they couldn’t get it to stop.

“How much blood is too much blood,” she asked.

The midwife told her to send a photo. Stephanie sent two, one of dried blood
on Gwen’s stomach and the other of a pile of bloodied tissues. The midwife
instructed Stephanie to tape some gauze over Gwen’s belly button. About 90
minutes later, just before going to bed, she checked on Gwen again. She
snapped another picture, this one with bright red blood soaking through the
gauze and diaper, and texted it to the midwife. “Are you sure this is fine?”

The midwife told her to go to the emergency room.

![A screenshot of a text message conversation dated Aug. 20, 2023, at 8:35
p.m. There are two green outgoing bubbles. One says, “So sorry to bother you
but quick question. Gwen’s belly button has started bleeding and it’s been
most of the day and we can’t get it to stop. How much blood is too much blood.
I called my mom and she suggested tissue with slight pressure but I don’t
think that worked.” The other says, “Do we need to do something else? Should I
put alcohol on it?” The incoming gray bubble responds, “Can you send me a
pic?”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/StephanieTexts_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=527)Stephanie
texted her midwife about Gwen’s bleeding before going to the emergency room.
Courtesy of the Biesenbach family

In many states, all emergency rooms are in hospitals, where patients can be
transferred to other units for more care. Not so in Texas, where more than 200
ERs are freestanding, separate and distinct from a hospital. At the ER, Gwen
grew increasingly pale. Her heart raced at 177 beats a minute. Around 1:40
a.m., Stephanie and Eric received their first piece of good news: Malouf was
transferring Gwen. She had scrapped her plan to send Gwen to the local
hospital and would instead transfer her to North Central Baptist, a larger
hospital in nearby San Antonio with more specialists. North Central was only
about half an hour away, and it was sending a NICU transport team to get Gwen.

Eric’s eyes fixated on the large clock hanging in the room. Ten minutes
passed, then 20, then 30, then an hour. He couldn’t understand what was taking
so long. He stepped into the hallway and asked if he could just drive Gwen to
the hospital.

But, he said, Malouf told him he couldn’t because it would be too dangerous.
Malouf, however, said she told him that if he did leave, he would have to sign
paperwork acknowledging he was doing so against medical advice. The transport
team, she told him, would have blood and IVs. Besides, she said, Gwen was
stable. Malouf called to check on the status of the ambulance; she was told
they were on their way.

Stephanie and Eric said that was the last time they spoke to Malouf that
night.

By the time the ambulance arrived, it had been nearly two hours since Malouf
had requested it. One of the team’s first questions was whether Gwen had
received a vitamin K shot.

The ER nurse told them they didn’t have the shot on hand.

It was the first time since walking into the ER, Stephanie said, that anyone
suggested that vitamin K may be the culprit — and the cure.

At 3:45 a.m., within minutes of the ambulance team’s arrival, they gave Gwen a
vitamin K shot in her left thigh. They spent the next two hours at her
bedside, hooking her up to an IV, drawing blood for lab tests and giving her
antibiotics — all things that, the records show, hadn’t been done yet. Malouf
didn’t respond to questions about why not.

Stephanie and Eric observed the ambulance team as they worked, bantering,
discussing another call that had come in and, just as they were about to
leave, waiting for one of them to go to the bathroom. Between what they viewed
as the team’s laidback pace and Malouf’s reassurances that Gwen was stable,
Stephanie and Eric were encouraged enough to split up. Eric went home to the
kids, who had been with his mom all night, to get them ready for their first
day of school. Stephanie stayed and planned to ride with Gwen in the
ambulance.

“Grab me a change of clothes and coffee,” Stephanie called to him as he was
leaving.

The team transferred Gwen to a temperature-controlled enclosed incubator. As
they packed up to leave, Gwen began to whimper. With each breath, Stephanie
said, she let out a weak, high-pitched sound. It was unnatural. Stephanie
reached through the incubator’s opening and ran her hands back and forth
across her daughter’s chest.  

The team loaded Gwen onto the ambulance and flipped on the sirens and lights.
At 5:55 a.m., they headed down Interstate 35. It had been seven hours since
Gwen was first admitted to the ER.

![A close-up photograph of an infant with dark, wispy hair; wide, dark eyes;
and an open-mouthed expression, resting against a gray fabric
surface.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/Attachment-1_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Gwen
Courtesy of the Biesenbach family ![A hand holds a cutout of a small ink
footprint print against a framed yellow surface containing other stamped
footprints.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/IMG_0264-2_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)A
cutout of Gwen’s footprint held next to that of one of her sisters Courtesy of
the Biesenbach family

* * *

Stephanie appreciated the importance of vitamin K. All of her other children
got the vitamin K shot shortly after they were born. But over the years, she
and her husband had grown wary of medical intervention. When their youngest
son was nearly 2, they fell behind on his vaccines. After getting several
vaccines at one appointment, they said, he developed a high fever and suddenly
stopped talking for about a year. He was later diagnosed with autism.

“I think that they just gave him too much at once,” Eric said.

Research studies from numerous sources have found that multiple vaccines taken
at once do not overwhelm or weaken a child’s immune system. They also do not
increase the risk of serious or long-term adverse effects.

Still, seeing their son struggle to speak, Stephanie and Eric were convinced
there was a connection. They stopped vaccinating their children after that.

Before Gwen’s birth, Stephanie’s midwife gave her a five-page handout on
newborn vitamin K. It covered why babies need vitamin K to help their blood
clot and cautioned that babies who don’t have enough of it can start to bleed
without warning.

The handout compared the pros and cons of the vitamin K shot with oral vitamin
K drops, noting that the drawbacks of the drops are that some babies may not
be able to absorb them or may spit them up. They also don’t eliminate the risk
of bleeding entirely. Stephanie initially signed the document agreeing to the
shot, but as her due date neared, she and Eric changed their minds. If both
are effective, they reasoned, why not go for the option that didn’t involve
sticking their baby with a needle?

“We did our own research. I don’t remember feeling like there were red flags,”
Stephanie said. “I felt like the information we had was sufficient.”

She doesn’t recall exactly what sources she consulted, but she read articles
online and spoke to some people who worked in the medical field. No one, she
said, warned her against the drops. But she didn’t ask her mother, Lauren
Hoel, a longtime family nurse practitioner. Stephanie knew exactly what her
mom would say.

Many medical experts consider the drops inferior for several reasons,
including those mentioned in the handout. There are also concerns about
harried parents of a newborn forgetting a dose and the fact that cases of
vitamin K deficiency bleeding have been reported even when drops are used.

Only limited data exists about vitamin K drops, and much of it is from Europe,
where the drops are more common. In the U.S., the Food and Drug Administration
does not provide oversight of the drops. Instead, parents can simply add them
to their Amazon carts without any verification of what’s in them, or whether
they’re safe or effective.

A single vitamin K shot acts quickly, and then the liver stores the rest of
the vitamin K to slowly release into the baby’s system over months.

For decades, the recommendation from doctors, hospitals and medical
organizations has been the shot. The Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the World Health
Organization call for giving the shot to all newborns.

“While some countries outside of the U.S. sometimes administer vitamin K
orally, it has not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration,” the
American Academy of Pediatrics [wrote in May](https://www.aap.org/en/news-
room/fact-checked/vitamin-k-helps-prevent-dangerous-bleeding-disorders-in-
newborns/?srsltid=AU7gw4Vqmb-QPwnKC4KD9ruHZ3v7ZUiTvYGjM4c2PxY0KluTdOCyumRB),
reiterating its longstanding position, “and it is less effective than an
intramuscular injection.”

Stephanie and Eric’s choice to opt for the drops reflects a broader trend.
Vaccine skepticism grew after the COVID-19 pandemic, and under the direction
of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a fierce vaccine
critic and champion of the Make America Healthy Again movement, the federal
government has fed those doubts. Stephanie and Eric, who voted for President
Donald Trump and are ardent supporters of both Kennedy and MAHA, welcomed the
change.

In December, the CDC stopped recommending that all newborns get the hepatitis
B vaccine. In January, the agency revised its childhood vaccination schedule,
reducing the number of routinely recommended shots by six. A federal judge
temporarily blocked that move in March, but the CDC’s decisions appear to have
caused a ripple effect beyond vaccines.

After the January change to the vaccine schedule, [an analysis of more than a
million newborns](https://www.truveta.com/blog/research/newborn-vitamin-k-non-
receipt-trends/) found a rise in the rate of babies not receiving the vitamin
K shot so sharp that it resembled a hockey stick. Between January and June of
this year, the analysis found, the rate jumped from 5.2% to 8.1%. Despite
being asked multiple times at a congressional hearing to assure parents that
the vitamin K shot is safe, Kennedy responded by declaring that he has not
said anything publicly about the shot. An HHS spokesperson did not answer
ProPublica’s questions but said that the CDC recommends that parents give
newborns the vitamin K shot within six hours of their birth to prevent vitamin
K deficiency bleeding.

![The exterior of a brick building that says “Baptist Children’s Hospital” set
against a clear blue sky.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260810-Bazan-
VitaminK-043_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)North
Central Baptist Hospital in San Antonio, where Gwen was transferred after
being treated at a standalone emergency room Brenda Bazán for ProPublica

* * *

In the ambulance, Gwen’s blood pressure dropped.

“Infant looks much more lethargic,” the team wrote in their notes.

They placed a mask on Gwen to increase her oxygen and gave her an infusion of
saline in hopes of improving her blood volume.

Gwen’s condition continued to deteriorate. Almost immediately after they
arrived at the hospital, her heart stopped. Doctors inserted a breathing tube
then began pressing down on her chest with two fingers to manually pump blood
through her body. They pushed epinephrine into her IV to stimulate her heart.
That appeared to work.

Stephanie couldn’t comprehend what was happening. All night, she said, no one
had acted like Gwen’s life was in danger. Suddenly, her daughter was covered
in tubes and doctors were performing CPR.

Stephanie said she heard someone yelling into a phone, “Where is the blood?”

She texted her family. “I need you to pray for Gwen like her life depends on
it,” she wrote.

She called Eric. “You need to get here now,” she told him.

Eric pressed on the gas pedal of Stephanie’s Honda and sped to the hospital.
There, he pushed through a clutch of doctors to find Stephanie crying in the
corner of the room. The same wave of shock that had washed over his wife
minutes earlier crashed over him. For the first time, he worried he might lose
his daughter.

They prayed together, and the chaplain stopped by the room to check on them.
He noted, according to records, that they were anxious but hopeful.

Less than two hours after she was admitted, Gwen crashed again. The medical
team called a code blue. Doctors performed CPR for the next 34 minutes. They
gave her epinephrine four more times. She had lost so much blood. Her heart
was barely pumping. Doctors told Stephanie and Eric that they could keep
trying to resuscitate Gwen or they could take her off the machines for her
parents to hold her.  

Stephanie sobbed. Eric collapsed at her knees. She told him she couldn’t make
the call. Eric said they wanted to spend the final moments with their
daughter. The doctors unhooked Gwen from the beeping machines and handed her
to him. Stephanie and Eric told Gwen how much they loved her and how much they
were going to miss her.

Shortly after 9 a.m., nearly 11 hours after they’d first brought her to the
ER, Gwen took her last breath. The team ushered them to another room where
families can mourn in private. They spent hours there. They gave Gwen a bath.
Family stopped by. Stephanie’s sister picked up their kids from school so they
could say goodbye to their baby sister. Two nurses came in to create molds of
Gwen’s hands and feet.

When Eric and Stephanie finally left the hospital, Gwen’s car seat was empty.
Their two youngest children slept in their bed that night. At one point,
Stephanie jolted awake. She turned to Eric. The look in his eyes told her that
it hadn’t been a dream. Without making a sound that could wake their kids,
they cried themselves back to sleep.

Eric’s grief soon morphed into anger. His brother-in-law drove him to the
Lonestar ER to ask for Gwen’s medical records. He didn’t trust himself to go
in, so he asked his brother-in-law to retrieve them.

The file was just 15 pages with the payment and registration forms. They
searched for any clue that could explain what happened to their daughter.

“I was constantly assured that it wasn’t that bad,” Eric said. “I can’t tell
you how many times they said, ‘Don’t worry, babies are very resilient.’”

They planned Gwen’s funeral. When they couldn’t find a coffin small enough to
fit her tiny 8-pound body, Eric’s brother, who makes custom cabinets, built
one. They wrapped Gwen in the flowered baby blanket from Stephanie’s
grandmother for the viewing.  

Stephanie and Eric operated on parallel tracks those next several months:
mourning their daughter and trying to understand what led to her death. The
family attended a grief camp put on by a local hospice group. They painted a
garden pole with things that reminded them of Gwen. When Thanksgiving
approached, they escaped to Stephanie’s sister’s house in Colorado to avoid
questions about how they were doing.

Eric got Gwen’s handprints tattooed on his chest, the last place he felt them
before she died. Stephanie picked Gwen’s footprints, but the tattoo artist had
to size them down to fit.

“She had such big feet,” Eric said. “She was gonna be a tall girl.”

“Or clown,” Stephanie said, half laughing, half crying. “One of the two.”

They also reached out to Byron Miller, a medical malpractice attorney, who
sought records from Malouf, the ER, the ambulance company and the hospital.
Miller investigated whether negligence in Gwen’s care resulted in her death.
But the medical expert hired to review the case homed in on Stephanie and
Eric’s decision to give Gwen the vitamin K drops instead of the shot. Without
an expert’s supporting opinion, which Miller said was a state requirement, his
office was unable to continue pursuing a case. Miller recommended that
Stephanie and Eric follow up with the Texas Medical Board.

The ER, the ambulance company and the hospital did not respond to multiple
requests for comment. The nurse on duty at Lonestar that night also did not
respond to requests for comment.

Stephanie had several conversations with her mother, who remembers learning in
the 1980s, while in nursing school, that all babies need a vitamin K shot at
birth. Hoel didn’t know that Stephanie and Eric didn’t get the vitamin K shot
for Gwen.

“It never occurred to me that people would refuse the vitamin K shot,” she
said.

Even with that, Hoel couldn’t look past Malouf’s actions that night.

“She should have said, ‘That’s a newborn. Take it to a NICU,’” Hoel said. “And
by not doing that, the fate was sealed.”

That next December, Stephanie sat down at the kitchen table and pulled out her
laptop. Someone, she said, had to hold Malouf accountable. She found the
website for the Texas Medical Board and followed the instructions to file a
complaint.

“When Dr Malouf decided to provide medical care to our daughter, despite her
lack of training in neonatal emergency care, and lack of appropriate
monitoring equipment,” Stephanie wrote to the board, “Gwen was deprived of any
potential life saving intervention.”

The seven hours they spent at the ER that night, she continued, could have
been used to save Gwen’s life. And she stressed that the ER nurse said the
facility didn’t carry the vitamin K injection.

“If Vitamin K was a vital part of the evening,” she wrote, “then we should
have been pointed to another location that was fully equipped sooner.”

Malouf became the target of her anger and her anguish. She described how
painful it was to drive by the Lonestar billboard with Malouf’s giant photo
near her house every day. She wrote that Malouf failed to recognize that her
daughter’s life was in danger. “I just don’t understand how it can go from a
calm relaxed environment to all of a sudden your child is dead,” she wrote to
the board. She recounted feeling intimidated when Eric asked if they could
leave when Gwen’s color began to change and Malouf advised against it.

“To this date,” she wrote, “Dr Nicole Malouf does not even know that my
daughter died under her care.”

![Potted plants and a decorative hand-painted wooden post stand in a grassy
yard under the shade of mature trees.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260810-Bazan-
VitaminK-027_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)A
garden pole the Biesenbachs made to memorialize Gwen stands in the family’s
yard. Brenda Bazán for ProPublica ![A folded floral quilt featuring an
embroidered green patch with a cross and the name Gwen rests on a gray
cushion.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20260810-Bazan-
VitaminK-022_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)A
baby blanket embroidered with the name Gwen was passed down by Stephanie’s
grandmother, Gwendolyn. Brenda Bazán for ProPublica

* * *

After Gwen died, Malouf said, a doctor from the hospital called. The news, she
said, came as a surprise.  

Sitting in her home office, her framed degrees hanging on the wall behind her,
Malouf spoke to ProPublica for nearly three hours about what happened. Malouf
and her husband have three daughters, for whom she is team mom for
cheerleading and president of the Fine Arts Boosters. Racks of uniforms filled
her home’s entryway in preparation for an upcoming sale.

She said she repeatedly relived the details of that night with her therapist.
The first few sessions, she said, were just the two of them crying. She said
they discussed what was in her control and what wasn’t. Every life is
precious, she said, but it’s one thing to lose a 95-year-old grandmother with
a long list of medical problems. It’s another to lose a baby.

“I still have my three daughters,” Malouf said, pushing back her long, dark
hair, “and now she has lost hers.”

Malouf said the doctor who called said the hospital would conduct its own
review. Malouf said the doctor mentioned that they had already identified some
issues, including questions about the transport team.

The hospital wasn’t the only one probing the night’s events. The state Medical
Board also launched an investigation. The board subpoenaed records and
reviewed the medical documents.

In September 2025, the board held a virtual hearing, which was closed to the
public. Stephanie and Eric appeared, as did Malouf and her attorney. The board
staff attorney charged that Malouf did not meet the standard of care in her
treatment of Gwen and that she failed to halt or limit Gwen’s bleeding. Her
lack of timely care, the board’s attorney alleged, ultimately resulted in
Gwen’s death. Citing confidentiality, the board would not release a recording
or transcript of the hearing.

The next month, the board issued its decision. It found that Malouf failed to
recognize that Gwen had a life-threatening vitamin K-dependent bleeding
disorder. The ER did not have vitamin K shots on site, and Malouf failed to
immediately transfer Gwen to a regional pediatric referral hospital better
equipped to handle Gwen’s condition. Finally, the board found that Malouf had
failed to quantify the amount of blood lost by Gwen.

![A document detailing findings from a medical board. Two findings are
highlighted in yellow: “Respondent failed to recognize that the patient had a
life-threatening Vitamin K dependent bleeding disorder,” and “Respondent’s
facility did not have Vitamin K injections on site and Respondent failed to
immediately transfer the patient to a regional pediatric referral hospital for
appropriate interventions.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/GwenDoc-V2_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)The
Texas medical board found that Dr. Nicole Malouf failed to recognize Gwen’s
vitamin K-dependent bleeding disorder and failed to immediately transfer her
to a pediatric hospital. Obtained and highlighted by ProPublica

The board required her to take 24 hours of continuing medical education; she
said she completed her hours in courses on pediatric advanced life support,
communicating with patients and vitamin K deficiency bleeding. She also had to
inform her employers that she had been disciplined. Malouf neither admitted
nor denied the allegations but agreed to abide by the board’s final order.

A board spokesperson would not answer specific questions about Gwen’s case but
said the board expects all licensees “to provide appropriate treatment and, if
the necessary supplies are not available, to make arrangements for transport
to a higher level of care.”

“I felt that I had done everything that I could with the resources I had,”
Malouf told ProPublica.

She said she did know that Gwen had vitamin K deficiency bleeding, even though
she did not immediately give Gwen a vitamin K shot. Malouf said she thinks the
board didn’t believe that she knew because she didn’t act “in a panicked
manner.” It remains unclear, even to her, whether the ER carried the vitamin K
shot at the time or if it was just in a spot where the nurse couldn’t find it.
But she said she asked the nurse for it.

Either way, she believed that giving Gwen vitamin K at that point would just
be to make her chart look good.

“It’s really not even going to take effect at that stage,” Malouf said. “As
soon as you give vitamin K, the earliest it’s even going to start working is
10 to 12 hours.”

But several doctors told ProPublica that vitamin K should be given immediately
if there’s even a suspicion that a baby has vitamin K deficiency bleeding.
It’s so vital to stopping the bleeding that they don’t even need to wait for a
confirmation. There is no downside, they said, to giving it. Vitamin K, they
said, may need to be followed up by blood or blood products, such as fresh
frozen plasma, which is rich in the proteins that help the blood clot.

While vitamin K can quickly help to halt the bleeding, it can’t reverse the
bleeding that’s already occurred. It also has to be given in time, and some
babies need more than one dose of vitamin K to recover. Gwen, as one doctor
who reviewed her medical records put it, needed vitamin K, blood and blood
products much sooner than she got them.

Malouf said she had learned about vitamin K deficiency bleeding in medical
school and during her residency, but she doesn’t recall ever seeing it in
practice. Nearly every medical student learns about the coagulation cascade,
but not all doctors know or remember how to diagnose and treat an infant who
shows up in an ER bleeding, often in the brain and invisible to the eye. Some
completed their training at a time when vitamin K deficiency bleeding was
still considered a historic condition, much like measles.

The ER staff, Malouf said, has been subsequently trained on the importance of
vitamin K, and the ER keeps it in stock. All ERs, she said, should carry
vitamin K.

“I still gravely regret that the outcome was still the same,” she said, “even
after again assuming that, ‘Hey, I’m putting this baby in y’all’s hands. You
guys are the experts. Fix her.’”

Malouf doesn’t understand how the board found that her care that night fell
short. She didn’t intentionally harm her patient.

“I can state my whole case and literally one of the board members goes, ‘Well,
I just don’t believe you,’” Malouf recalled. “I said, ‘Well, then I don’t know
what more to tell you.’”

In addition to working at the ER, she had a part-time job doing telehealth.
The telehealth company that employed her, she said, fired her once she
disclosed the board’s action. As of August, she was still working some shifts
at Lonestar ER; the board’s decision didn’t affect her ability to practice.
Following the interview with ProPublica, she declined further comment.

“I feel like the only way to change the outcome is to go back to the
beginning, that fork in the road,” Malouf said. “And go, ‘OK, well let’s give
vitamin K after birth.”

* * *

Stephanie and Eric also have asked themselves what they would have done
differently. They wished they had left the ER that night and driven Gwen to a
hospital.

“We were just trusting that the person who went to school their whole life for
this would know more than us,” Eric said.

In their minds, the role of vitamin K has overshadowed the medical mistakes
they believe are most responsible for their daughter’s death. By the time Gwen
had arrived at the hospital, her organs were already starting to shut down.
The autopsy found that she had tiny spots of bleeding in her kidneys and small
intestine and a small scrape on her chest where doctors pushed down for CPR.
The medical examiner noted Gwen’s precipitous decline and listed her cause of
death as vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

If they could go back, both agreed they would get the vitamin K shot for Gwen.

“I don’t trust a lot of things,” Stephanie said, “but get peace of mind and
get the vitamin K shot.”

A few months after Gwen’s death, Stephanie found out she was pregnant with a
little girl. They were so ready to love a baby again. She gave birth to her in
2024. This summer, they welcomed another baby girl.

Both got vitamin K shots.
